archetype.name: Super Bowl Contender (offense-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose 6-1 record rests on the league's best net efficiency, built on an elite pass-protecting, run-blocking offense and a defense that smothers the run, with the depth and health to make a deep January run if the bye fixes its injury list.

report.headline: The efficiency is real this time; the turnovers and kicking game aren't sustainable flaws
report.take:
This is the Shanahan machine at full power again. The 49ers lead the league in net EPA at 0.194, rank second in offensive EPA and first in offensive success rate, and Brock Purdy has started every game behind a line that has allowed only 7 sacks, the fewest in football. The run game isn't flashy in yards, but its 0.511 success rate leads the league, so the offense stays on schedule and the play-action passing game, second in EPA per dropback, does the damage. On defense the identity is narrower but sharp: second in rush EPA allowed, best in explosive runs allowed, third in explosive passes allowed. Teams have to drive the length of the field against them.

That matters for reading the record, because this is a different 6-1 from last year's 12-5. In 2025 the 49ers won 12 games with a net EPA that ranked 15th and 2.62 wins over expected. That was a team outrunning its play. This year the efficiency sits at the top of the league, the same tier as the 2022 and 2023 teams. There is still some good fortune in the record: they are perfect in one-score games, carry 1.68 wins over expected, and their point differential implies something closer to 4.3 wins. But the underlying team is closer to a 6-1 team than to a lucky one.

What the numbers hide is a slide that runs alongside the injury report. The two biggest passing games came against Miami and Arizona, defenses that now rank 31st and 27th. Against the better units, Seattle (5th) and Atlanta (8th), the passing game was close to break-even or worse. Most of the season's ten giveaways came in the last three games, including four in the loss at Atlanta. That stretch also brought hamstring injuries to Christian McCaffrey and Deebo Samuel, Mike Evans' Achilles tendinitis, and Nick Bosa's knee. Bosa has appeared in only two games. The other drag is special teams, 31st at -3.26 EPA a game, which is why some of these wins were closer than the offense deserved.

The bye arrives at the right time. McCaffrey and Evans are expected back, and Bosa and Samuel have a chance. A healthy version of this roster is the best team in the NFC on paper, and the NFC West lead is already comfortable. The remaining tests that will show whether the recent dip was injuries or something real are Minnesota's top-ranked defense, Kansas City on the road, and two division games against Seattle and the Rams.

strengths.title: Protection and an on-schedule run game
strengths.body: The line has allowed 7 sacks, the fewest in the league, along with a top-three pressure rate and a run game that leads the NFL in success rate. It isn't a product of game script: the offense passes a bit more than expected and still stays clean. Shanahan offenses with this line profile have historically held up, so this should last.

strengths.title: Elite efficiency, not just results
strengths.body: They lead the league in net EPA and rank second in passing EPA, which puts them back in the tier of the 2022-23 teams rather than last year's lucky 12-win team. Some of the passing efficiency was inflated by soft early opponents. Even so, efficiency is the stickiest thing a team carries into the second half.

strengths.title: A defense that removes big plays
strengths.body: The 49ers rank first in rush EPA allowed and first in explosive runs allowed, and third in explosive passes allowed. Opponents have to string together long drives, and that holds up even with Bosa playing only two games. If he returns, the pass rush, already eighth in pressure rate, gets a real ceiling.

concerns.title: Recent turnover spike
concerns.body: The offense has 10 giveaways and a minus-3 turnover margin, and most of that came in the last three games, including four in the loss at Atlanta. The timing lines up with McCaffrey, Evans and Samuel all getting banged up, which points to a thinned-out receiving group rather than a Purdy problem. Expect it to settle, but it is the main way this team loses games.

concerns.title: Special teams bleeding points
concerns.body: At -3.26 EPA a game, the 49ers rank 31st on special teams. That helps explain why an offense this efficient kept playing one-score games. It is a genuine flaw rather than a cost of anything else, and it matters most in close playoff-type games.

concerns.title: Close-game record will cool
concerns.body: A perfect one-score record and 1.68 wins over expected mean the point differential implies roughly two fewer wins than the 49ers have. The efficiency says they are good, but they won't keep winning every coin flip. The short-area pass defense, 24th in short EPA allowed, is where those close games get uncomfortable.

trend.note: The offense peaked against weak defenses in Weeks 2-3, then saw its passing EPA cool sharply against better units while turnovers piled up, ending in the Atlanta loss. The bye and returning starters are the likely correction.

nextGame.headline: Rested, healthier 49ers host a Raiders team that can't run
nextGame.body:
This sets up well for San Francisco. The Raiders' defense generates pressure (second in pressure rate) and takes the ball away (12 takeaways, second in the league). It is also among the worst at stopping short passes and finishing drives: 32nd in short-pass EPA allowed and 29th in red-zone TD rate allowed. The 49ers have the protection to neutralize the rush and the underneath game to exploit the soft middle. Las Vegas can throw with Kirk Cousins (seventh in pass EPA), but its run game is close to nonexistent, 31st in run EPA and last in yards before contact. Facing the league's best run defense, that makes the Raiders one-dimensional. The Book has SF -10 with a 51.5 total. Las Vegas has been the league's best cover team, so the margin is less certain than the result.

Availability is the bigger story for San Francisco, which comes off 14 days of rest. McCaffrey (hamstring) and Evans (Achilles) are expected back. Bosa (knee) and Samuel (hamstring) each have a chance, and S Marques Sigle and CB Upton Stout are questionable. Stout matters given the short-area coverage issues. For Las Vegas, CB Darien Porter left the Jets game with a groin injury and is questionable, and TE Carter Runyon and DE Patrick Johnson are on IR.

waysToWin.title: Work the underneath game to Kittle and McCaffrey
waysToWin.body: The Raiders allow more short-pass EPA than anyone, and tight ends draw a heavy share of the targets against them. With Kittle as the target leader and McCaffrey back, the 49ers can live in the short areas while their line handles Las Vegas' pressure. A lead back has also scored well above his usual output against this defense.

waysToWin.title: Make the Raiders one-dimensional
waysToWin.body: Las Vegas cannot run the ball: 31st in run EPA and last in yards before contact. San Francisco is first in rush EPA allowed. Taking away the run turns every down into an obvious passing down for Cousins.

waysToWin.title: Finish drives with touchdowns
waysToWin.body: The Raiders give up touchdowns on most red-zone trips, 29th in the league. San Francisco's first-ranked success rate should keep producing those trips, and converting them builds the kind of margin its weak special teams can't erase.

waysToLose.title: Another turnover-fest against ballhawks
waysToLose.body: The Raiders rank second in takeaways and second in pressure rate, and San Francisco just gave the ball away four times at Atlanta. If the giveaways continue, short fields turn a 10-point favorite into a coin flip.

waysToLose.title: Cousins carves the short middle
waysToLose.body: Las Vegas passes efficiently, and San Francisco is 24th in short-pass EPA allowed and soft against slot receivers. With Stout and Sigle questionable, a quick-game plan could let the Raiders keep pace in a shootout.

waysToLose.title: Special teams hands back field position
waysToLose.body: A 31st-ranked special teams unit has kept games closer than they should be. Combined with a Raiders team that has covered most of its games, a few hidden-yardage swings could make this uncomfortable late.

nextGame.watch: Whether Purdy's ball security returns with McCaffrey and Evans back against a Raiders defense built on pressure and takeaways.

restOfSeason.body:
The foundation is sustainable. Top-ranked protection, a league-best run success rate and an elite run defense are the kinds of traits that carry over week to week, and history shows this staff's efficient teams stay efficient. What will regress is the perfect one-score record. The schedule also stiffens, with Minnesota's No. 1 defense, Kansas City on the road, and the Rams and Seahawks in the division, so expect a handful of losses. Some of those likely come in games decided by turnovers or special teams.

The upside case is health. A healthy McCaffrey and Evans should restore the passing game that cooled while they were hurting, and a Bosa return gives a good pass rush a true closer. The division lead is already big enough that a top playoff seed is the realistic goal rather than just a playoff berth.
swingFactors: Nick Bosa's knee and how much he plays
Health of McCaffrey, Evans and Samuel
Whether the recent turnover spike fades

confidence.note: Seven games, but efficiency ranks are elite and consistent with past peak seasons; several injuries cloud the picture.
